title: The BBC Prison Study
text:
In 2002 the social psychologists Stephen Reicher and Alex Haslam ran a new prison study with the BBC, filmed for television and overseen by an ethics committee. Fifteen men were divided into guards and prisoners in a purpose-built setting. Unlike at Stanford, the researchers did not tell the guards how to behave. They only watched and measured what happened.

The guards did not slide into cruelty. Many were uneasy about using their authority and could not agree among themselves. The prisoners, by contrast, built a strong shared identity, challenged the guards and eventually broke the system. The groups then formed a self-governing commune.

But the commune also struggled, and some members grew frustrated with its disorder. A few former prisoners and guards then proposed a new, harsher regime with themselves in firm control, and others showed growing support for it. At that point the study was ended. Reicher and Haslam argued that tyranny did not come from people simply stepping into roles. It became attractive when groups failed and people longed for someone to impose order.
lesson: Strong-handed rule tends to win support when groups feel chaotic and powerless. A leader who keeps a group functioning and united does more to prevent tyranny than one who only preaches against it.
source: Reicher, S., and Haslam, S. A. (2006). Rethinking the psychology of tyranny: The BBC prison study. British Journal of Social Psychology, 45(1), 1-40.
caveat: It was a single study made for television, with a small sample, so its conclusions are suggestive rather than definitive.
